Source: (Zuboy et al. 2022, 2023) Also illustrated in Figure 8 is the adoption of bifacial module technologies. For residential applications using monofacial modules, bifacial cells can be placed on white or black backsheets. More commonly, bifacial cells are placed in modules with transparent back glass or a transparent backsheet. Globally, bifacial c-Si cells accounted for less than 3% of the market in 2015 (Cellere et al. 2016) and are projected to have greater than 90% market share in 2024, including cells for utility and residential applications (Fischer et al. 2025). The United States was an early adopter of bifacial c-Si technologies for technological reasons (including improvements in system power production) and trade policy reasons. Beginning in 2018, all c-Si cells and modules imported into the United States were tariffed at 30%, with a scheduled phase down to 15% in 2021 (Pickerel 2021). Bifacial modules were granted a full exemption from these Section 201 tariffs in 2019 (Pickerel 2019) in large part because bifacial modules were most applicable to utility-scale applications, and U.S. manufacturing was producing PV modules for distributed PV applications. The exemption was repealed in 2020, reinstated in 2021, and finally removed in 2024 (Pickerel 2024b). Until February 2026, all imported c-Si modules (regardless of bifaciality or country of origin, with a few minor exceptions) are tariffed at 14.25% under Section 201 of the Trade Act (U.S. International Trade Administration 2025b). Analysis of U.S. Customs and Border Protection data found that 42% of modules imported into the United States were bifacial in 2020, and 82% were bifacial in 2023 (Pickerel 2024b; U.S. International Trade Administration 2025b). Analysis of the California and New York distributed PV databases (NYSERDA 2025; California Public Utilities Commission 2025) found that less than 10% of distributed systems larger than 5 MW dc installed in 2020 were bifacial, but constituted 80% of those sized systems installed in 2024 (vs. 5% of systems with capacities of 2.5–10 kW ). dc 11 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2.3.2 Domestic Production of Crystalline-Silicon Modules PV Tech reported that in 2024 the United States produced 7.6 GW of c-Si modules (up 155%, dc year over year), with an NLR-estimated year-end U.S. module assembly capacity of 41.0 GW ,9 dc up 488% year over year ( PV Tech Research 2025); NLR estimates that there was an additional 9.1 GW of manufacturing capacity under construction at the end of 2024, of which 3.5 GW dc dc came online in the first half of 2025.10 At the same time, 1.4 GW of U.S. manufacturing dc capacity went offline in the first half of 2025 when
